title: India Just Waived Seven Years of Nuclear Import Duties. The Iran War Made It Urgent.
excerpt: A finance ministry order retroactively clears customs on reactor equipment back to 2019 and extends duty-free status through 2035, signalling that energy independence has become a national security priority.
body:
India has quietly waived customs duties on all equipment imported for nuclear power generation going back seven years, in a move that signals just how urgently the Iran war has made energy independence a matter of national security.

The finance ministry order, dated June 11, grants retrospective exemptions on nuclear power equipment imports made between April 1, 2019 and January 31, 2026. It extends a policy announced in the February budget, which exempted nuclear imports from customs duty through 2035 — but now applies it backward, retroactively clearing duties already assessed on billions of rupees worth of reactor components, turbines, and specialised materials.

The timing is not coincidental. Three months into a war that has all but closed the Strait of Hormuz, India's energy security vulnerabilities have never been more exposed.

The Oil Dependency Problem

India imports approximately 85 per cent of its crude oil. When Iran curtailed shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in March, Brent crude spiked past $93 a barrel. The government's fertiliser subsidy bill doubled. The fiscal deficit is now expected to widen to 4.8 per cent of GDP — half a percentage point above the February target. The rupee has been under sustained pressure, touching 95.76 against the dollar on Thursday.

Every one of these problems traces back to a single structural weakness: India generates 55 per cent of its electricity from coal and depends on imported oil and gas for the rest. Nuclear power currently accounts for just 3.2 per cent of India's total electricity generation — roughly 7,500 megawatts of installed capacity across seven operational plants.

The government wants to change that dramatically. India's nuclear programme targets 22,480 MW by 2031, with longer-term ambitions to reach 63,000 MW under an expanded plan that includes both pressurised heavy water reactors built domestically and light water reactors constructed with Russian and French technology.

What the Waiver Does

The retrospective exemption is unusual because it effectively refunds duties that nuclear operators — primarily the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) — had already paid on imported equipment. This includes reactor pressure vessels, steam generators, instrumentation systems, and specialised nuclear-grade materials that India cannot yet manufacture domestically.

The forward-looking exemption through 2035 gives nuclear developers a clear customs-free runway for the next decade. Together, the two measures remove a significant cost barrier for the massive reactor expansion India is planning.

NPCIL currently has ten reactors under construction, including two 1,000 MW units at Kudankulam in Tamil Nadu built with Russian technology and the first 700 MW pressurised heavy water reactor at Gorakhpur in Haryana.

The government has also approved sites for six nuclear parks, each designed to house multiple reactors, across states including Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Andhra Pradesh.

Three Geopolitical Forces

India's nuclear push sits at the intersection of three converging pressures.

First, the Iran war has demonstrated that any country dependent on seaborne oil imports is vulnerable to the politics of a single strait. India's refiners have scrambled to secure crude through August by diversifying supply routes, but the underlying exposure remains. Nuclear generation is immune to shipping lane disruptions.

Second, India's climate commitments require a massive expansion of non-fossil electricity. Nuclear is the only baseload zero-carbon technology that can scale to the levels India needs without the intermittency challenges of solar and wind. The country aims to reach 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030 — an ambitious target that solar alone cannot meet reliably.

Third, the US-India Civil Nuclear Agreement of 2008, which ended India's decades-long isolation from global nuclear commerce, is finally bearing operational fruit. The customs waiver signals that New Delhi wants to accelerate the flow of technology and materials that the agreement was designed to enable.

The Small Modular Reactor Question

India is also watching the global race in small modular reactors closely. The technology, which promises faster construction times and lower upfront capital costs, could be particularly suited to India's need for distributed power generation across a vast geography. The Department of Atomic Energy has been studying designs from multiple international vendors, though no formal procurement has been announced.

The customs waiver, by covering "all goods imported for nuclear power generation" without specifying reactor type, appears broad enough to encompass SMR components if India decides to pursue that path.

Why NRIs Should Care

For the Indian diaspora, the nuclear push matters on multiple levels. NRI engineers and scientists have been instrumental in India's nuclear programme since its inception. Several Indian-Americans work in the US nuclear industry and could play a role in future technology transfer.

More practically, India's energy mix directly affects cost of living, inflation, and economic growth back home. Every percentage point of electricity shifted from imported fossil fuels to domestic nuclear generation reduces India's vulnerability to the oil price shocks that have battered the economy this year.

The customs waiver is a technical order buried in the Official Gazette. But what it says is straightforward: India is betting that the next decade of energy security will be built on uranium, not oil.
